insight.title: How trees whisper to one another
insight.subtitle: The silent conversation happening beneath your feet

sections.text: Walk through a quiet forest and you might assume the stillness is absolute. But beneath the soft moss and damp earth, a hidden world is pulsing with life. The trees are not solitary giants standing alone. They are deeply connected, sharing stories and secrets through a vast, invisible web that links every root.

This network relies on tiny fungal threads that act like fiber-optic cables. Through these strands, older trees send sugar and water to struggling saplings in the shade. They even trade chemical warnings about approaching insects. It is a slow, rhythmic pulse of generosity that ensures the entire forest thrives together rather than competing.

Nature reminds us that strength is rarely a solo endeavor. Even the tallest oak relies on the quiet support of its neighbors to survive the storm. When we look at the woods, we see more than just timber and leaves. We see a blueprint for community, where survival depends entirely on the beauty of staying connected.

news.title: Frustrated Lewis pair chemistry enables dual atom insertion to build bioactive molecules
news.description: Researchers from the National University of Singapore (NUS) have developed a boron-catalyzed method to transform oxetanes, which are small four-membered ring molecules, into larger, medicinally relevant 1,3-oxazinanes by the selective insertion of two building blocks, a carbon unit and a nitrogen unit. The research team was led by Associate Professor Koh Ming Joo from the NUS Department of Chemistry. The research breakthrough was published in the journal Nature Synthesis on March 12, 2026.

news.title: To shed light on how the human brain ages, study reveals new insights from mice
news.description: By scanning the brains of mice throughout their lifespans, scientists at Columbia's Zuckerman Institute and the University of Texas at Dallas have discovered that the human brain is not unique in how it changes with age. These findings might one day help researchers pinpoint mechanisms in humans that confer vulnerability to, or grant resilience from, age-related brain decline, diseases and disorders. Their research is published in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.
